outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic initiative that would have imposed a tax on the windfall profits oil companies have reaped from rising energy prices, with the minority leader dismissing the proposal as a “gimmick.”

Record energy prices have translated into record profits for oil companies. The measure failed to secure the 60 votes required under Senate rules to advance, with the vote ending 51-43. Six Republicans, including three facing re-election in November, broke ranks to support the bill. Two Democrats opposed it: Sen. Mary Landrieu of the oil-producing state of Louisiana, and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who voted no in order to preserve his ability under Senate rules to bring the measure back to the floor.

In addition to imposing a special 25 percent tax on oil companies, the bill would have allowed lawsuits against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the oil-producing cartel, and suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Profits derived from renewable energy sources would have been excluded from the tax.

“We’re not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing,” said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. “And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us.

“We’re not afraid to do some strong tough things that will — some in the short run, some in the longer run — that will bring down the price, the all too high price, of gasoline.”

Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, said the measure was necessary to “wring out” speculators, whom he blamed for driving the price of crude oil above $130 a barrel in recent weeks.

Senate Republicans, however, insisted that the new taxes would ultimately harm consumers and reduce the American oil supply, accusing Democrats of engaging in election-year politics.

The bill is “pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan,” said Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said, “Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won’t address the problem. This bill isn’t a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick.”

The Kentucky Republican added, “They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade.”

As the average price of gasoline edged above $4 a gallon, high fuel costs were clearly weighing on voters. A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll released Tuesday showed that 40 percent of respondents were more concerned about the cost of gasoline than about long lines at the pump, such as those that occurred during the energy crisis of the 1970s. However, 55 percent of those surveyed said they were more worried about long lines and rationing.

The poll results are based on telephone interviews with 1,035 adults conducted Wednesday and Thursday. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

CNN’s Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Tuesday, Senate Republicans stopped a Democratic-backed proposal that sought to impose a tax on the unusually large profits oil companies have made as energy prices have climbed. The chamber’s minority leader dismissed the plan as a “gimmick.”

Oil companies have posted record earnings amid historically high energy prices. But the proposal did not receive the 60 votes needed under Senate procedure to move forward, falling short in a 51-43 vote.

Six Republicans voted in favor of the legislation, including three who were facing re-election campaigns in November. Two Democrats opposed it: Sen. Mary Landrieu of Louisiana, a major oil-producing state, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid. Reid voted no so that, under Senate rules, he could later bring the measure up again.

The bill would have imposed a 25 percent special tax on oil companies. It also would have allowed legal action against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the oil-producing cartel known as OPEC, and would have halted additions to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Earnings from renewable energy would not have been subject to the tax.

Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York, said Democrats were willing to confront both major oil companies and OPEC.

“We’re not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing,” Schumer said. “And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us.”

He added that Democrats were prepared to take “strong tough” steps, some with short-term effects and others with longer-term results, to reduce what he called the “all too high” price of gasoline.

Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, argued that the bill was necessary to “wring out” speculators, whom he blamed for helping push crude oil prices above $130 a barrel in recent weeks.

Republicans in the Senate countered that the proposed taxes would ultimately harm consumers and reduce domestic oil supplies. They accused Democrats of using the issue for political advantage in an election year.

Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas, called the bill “pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan.”

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said targeting gasoline companies might be useful for campaign materials or television news coverage, but would not solve the underlying problem.

“This bill isn’t a serious response to gas prices,” McConnell said. “It is just a gimmick.”

The Kentucky Republican also accused Democrats of trying to appear active on the issue after supporting legislation he said would worsen the situation.

“They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse,” McConnell said. “What a political charade.”

With the national average price of gasoline moving above $4 per gallon, fuel costs have become a major concern for voters. A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey released Tuesday found that 40 percent of respondents were more worried about gasoline prices than about the possibility of long lines at gas stations, such as those seen during the 1970s energy crisis.

However, 55 percent of those polled said they were more concerned about long lines and rationing.

The poll was conducted by telephone with 1,035 adults on Wednesday and Thursday. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

CNN’s Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic proposal aimed at taxing oil companies’ windfall profits at a time of record-high energy prices and strong industry earnings. The measure failed to advance after falling short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a procedural hurdle, with the final vote coming in at 51-43.

The legislation would have imposed a 25 percent tax on certain oil company profits deemed excessive. It also included provisions that would have allowed lawsuits against OPEC for actions affecting oil markets and would have suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Democrats argued that the bill was necessary to hold major oil companies accountable during a period of high gasoline prices. They said the proposal would target “Big Oil,” limit the influence of OPEC, and help bring down costs for consumers at the pump.

Republicans rejected the measure, calling it an election-year gimmick. They argued that imposing new taxes on oil companies would ultimately increase costs for consumers, discourage domestic energy production, and reduce the American oil supply. The failed vote underscored the sharp partisan divide in Congress over how to respond to high energy prices and the role of oil companies in the broader economy.

Senate Democrats pushed a broad energy bill aimed at responding to record gasoline prices and soaring oil-company profits, but the measure was blocked by Senate Republicans in a procedural vote.

The proposal would have imposed a 25 percent windfall-profits tax on major oil companies, allowed the Justice Department to sue OPEC members for price manipulation, and temporarily stopped deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Democrats argued that the legislation was needed to curb excessive profits, discourage market manipulation, and provide relief to consumers facing historically high prices at the pump.

The bill also reflected growing public frustration over the gap between rising household energy costs and the large profits reported by major oil producers. Supporters said companies benefiting from high crude prices should either invest more in domestic production, refining capacity, and renewable energy or face additional taxes on what Democrats described as unreasonable profits.

Republicans opposed the measure, saying it would not lower gasoline prices and could instead reduce domestic energy investment. They argued that higher taxes on oil companies would likely be passed on to consumers and would discourage the production and refining needed to increase supply. GOP senators said Congress should focus instead on expanding domestic drilling, easing restrictions on exploration, and increasing energy production.

The measure received 51 votes in favor and 43 against, falling short of the 60 votes required to move forward under Senate rules. The failed vote highlighted the deep partisan divide over how best to respond to high energy prices: Democrats focused on oil-company profits and market oversight, while Republicans emphasized increasing supply and avoiding new taxes on the energy industry.

With the bill blocked, Congress remained deadlocked over a federal response to rising fuel costs, even as gasoline prices continued to place pressure on consumers and became a major political issue.

counterfactuals.output:
**Senate Republicans block Democratic windfall-profits tax on oil companies as gas prices climb**

**WASHINGTON** — Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic proposal to impose a windfall-profits tax on major oil companies, derailing the measure as lawmakers faced growing pressure from voters angry over record gasoline prices.

The vote was **51-43**, short of the **60 votes** needed to advance the bill. Most Democrats supported moving ahead with the legislation, while Republicans largely opposed it, arguing that higher taxes on oil producers would do little to lower prices at the pump and could discourage domestic energy production.

The Democratic measure would have placed a tax on what supporters described as “excessive” profits by the largest oil companies, while also rolling back certain tax breaks and aiming to curb market speculation. Democrats framed the bill as a response to soaring fuel costs and record earnings reported by major oil firms.

Senate Democratic leaders said the vote showed Republicans were siding with the oil industry over consumers.

“At a time when families are being squeezed every time they fill up their tanks, the Senate had a chance to hold Big Oil accountable,” Democrats argued. “Instead, Republicans blocked it.”

Republicans countered that the proposal amounted to a political messaging bill that would not increase supply or reduce gasoline prices.

“This is not a serious energy policy,” GOP opponents said, warning that a windfall-profits tax could “punish production” and ultimately lead to higher costs.

The vote came as gasoline prices were a dominant economic and political issue. National average prices had climbed to around **$4 a gallon**, intensifying criticism of both Congress and the White House. Democrats sought to focus public anger on oil companies’ profits, while Republicans blamed Democrats for blocking expanded drilling and other domestic energy measures.

Polling at the time suggested the Democratic argument had public appeal. A **CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll** found broad support for taxing oil companies’ windfall profits, with a sizable majority of Americans saying they favored such a move amid rising gasoline prices. But the same polling environment also showed voters deeply frustrated with Washington’s handling of energy costs, giving both parties incentives to use the issue in the broader election-year fight.

The White House had threatened to veto the legislation if it reached the president’s desk, calling it the wrong approach to energy prices. With Republicans able to block the bill in the Senate, the proposal never advanced that far.

Democrats said they would continue pressing for measures aimed at oil company profits and market speculation. Republicans said the answer was more domestic production, fewer regulations and a broader energy strategy.

The defeat underscored the sharp partisan divide over how to respond to rising gasoline prices — and ensured that energy costs would remain a central issue on Capitol Hill and in the campaign debate.

counterfactuals.output:
**Fictional political news report — Washington**

**Senate Bill Targeting Big Oil Profits, OPEC Lawsuits and Strategic Petroleum Reserve Fails Amid Partisan Clash**

**WASHINGTON —** A closely watched Senate energy bill aimed at curbing major oil company profits, authorizing lawsuits against OPEC members and restricting use of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve failed to advance Tuesday after lawmakers split sharply over whether the proposal would lower gasoline prices or deepen political divisions over energy policy.

The measure, backed by Democratic leaders, fell short of the votes needed to overcome a procedural hurdle, effectively shelving the package for now. The bill would have imposed new penalties on what supporters described as “excessive” oil company profits, strengthened legal tools to challenge alleged price-fixing by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, and tightened rules governing releases from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., blamed Republicans for blocking what he called a necessary response to high fuel costs and industry windfalls.

“Families are paying the price while Big Oil posts record profits,” Schumer said in this fictional account. “This bill was about accountability — accountability for oil companies, accountability for foreign producers who manipulate supply, and accountability in how we manage our emergency reserves.”

Former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., a longtime critic of oil industry concentration and OPEC pricing power, argued that Congress had a responsibility to confront both domestic and international drivers of price spikes.

“We cannot simply shrug while consumers get squeezed at the pump,” Dorgan said. “If OPEC acts like a cartel, the United States should have the ability to challenge it. And if oil companies are profiting from crisis conditions, the public deserves answers.”

Republicans countered that the bill relied on political messaging rather than increased domestic production. They argued that windfall-profit penalties would discourage investment, that lawsuits against OPEC could provoke diplomatic and market retaliation, and that limits on the Strategic Petroleum Reserve could reduce presidential flexibility during emergencies.

Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas, said the measure would hurt energy-producing states and risk making supply problems worse.

“This bill goes after the very producers we need to bring more energy to market,” Hutchison said. “Punishing American energy companies will not produce one additional barrel of oil, and tying the hands of policymakers on the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is not a serious energy strategy.”

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., called the proposal “a political exercise” and said Democrats were avoiding what he described as the core issue: supply.

“The American people want lower prices, not lawsuits, tax hikes and press conferences,” McConnell said. “If Washington wants to bring down energy costs, it should make it easier to produce, refine and transport American energy.”

The debate revived long-running arguments over how much influence Congress can exert over gasoline prices. Supporters said the bill would deter profiteering and give U.S. officials more leverage over foreign oil producers. Opponents said global oil markets are complex and that punitive measures could reduce investment or destabilize supply.

The provision targeting OPEC drew particular attention. Similar proposals, often referred to as “NOPEC” legislation, have circulated in Congress for years. They seek to amend antitrust law to allow the Justice Department to sue foreign oil-producing nations for coordinated production decisions. Presidents of both parties have historically been cautious about such efforts, warning they could disrupt diplomatic relationships with key energy-producing countries.

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve provisions also sparked disagreement. Democrats said clearer limits were needed to ensure the reserve is used for genuine emergencies and not manipulated for political purposes. Republicans said the administration should retain flexibility to respond quickly to wars, natural disasters or severe supply disruptions.

Energy analysts said the bill’s failure was unsurprising given the election-year politics surrounding gasoline prices and the regional divide between oil-producing and oil-consuming states.

For now, the defeat leaves Congress without a clear path forward on energy-price legislation. Democratic leaders indicated they may try to revive parts of the package, while Republicans said they would continue pressing for expanded drilling, faster permitting and infrastructure approvals.

Schumer said the issue would not disappear.

“The vote may be over, but the problem remains,” he said. “We are going to keep fighting for consumers who are tired of being told there is nothing Washington can do.”

McConnell signaled that any future compromise would need to move away from taxes and legal actions.

“If Democrats want a serious conversation, Republicans are ready,” he said. “But it has to start with producing more American energy.”

counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON —** Congress’s election-year fight over soaring gasoline prices and record oil company profits intensified Tuesday as Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic energy measure aimed at punishing large petroleum companies and shifting federal policy toward conservation and alternative fuels.

The Democratic proposal, advanced as motorists faced gasoline prices near historic highs, would have repealed tax breaks for major oil companies, imposed new penalties on companies earning “excessive” profits while failing to invest in new energy production or renewable fuels, and strengthened federal authority to pursue price manipulation and oil market speculation. It also included provisions targeting OPEC by allowing the Justice Department to pursue antitrust action against oil-producing nations accused of colluding to restrict supply.

But the measure fell short of the 60 votes needed to advance, as nearly all Republicans opposed it. GOP senators called the bill a political response that would do little to increase supply or lower prices at the pump. Democrats, meanwhile, accused Republicans of protecting an industry that has reported billions of dollars in quarterly profits while families and businesses struggle with fuel costs.

“Americans are paying the price every time they fill up their tanks, while the largest oil companies are posting record profits,” one Democratic supporter said during debate. “Congress has a responsibility to end unnecessary subsidies and demand accountability from companies that are benefiting from this crisis.”

Republicans countered that the Democratic plan focused on taxes and lawsuits rather than production. They said higher taxes on oil companies would discourage investment, reduce domestic supply and potentially drive prices higher. GOP lawmakers pushed instead for expanded offshore drilling, access to oil reserves in Alaska and other federal lands, and faster permitting for refineries and energy infrastructure.

“This bill is not an energy plan,” a Republican opponent said. “It is a tax increase dressed up as consumer protection. If we want lower prices, we need more American energy.”

The clash underscored the sharp divide between the parties over how to respond to public anger about gasoline prices. Democrats have sought to portray oil companies as profiting from consumers’ pain, pointing to earnings reports from major firms that have shown huge profits amid elevated crude prices. They argue that federal subsidies enacted years earlier are no longer justified and that Congress should redirect incentives toward renewable energy, efficiency and consumer relief.

Republicans have framed the issue as a supply problem, arguing that domestic production has been constrained by Democratic opposition to drilling. They say Congress should remove barriers to exploration and production rather than penalize companies that already face high global demand and geopolitical uncertainty.

The White House had also signaled opposition to the Democratic measure, warning that new taxes and legal exposure for energy producers could harm investment and fail to provide near-term relief for drivers.

The blocked bill included several provisions Democrats said were designed to respond directly to public frustration. Among them were efforts to roll back tax benefits for the biggest oil companies, create a windfall-profits penalty for companies that did not invest in renewable energy or expanded production, and give regulators additional tools to police energy trading markets. Supporters said speculation in oil futures had contributed to price spikes, though analysts have debated how much of the increase stemmed from financial trading versus global supply-and-demand pressures.

Oil industry representatives opposed the proposal, saying companies’ profits reflected the scale of their operations and the global price of crude oil, not manipulation. They warned that punitive taxes could reduce exploration budgets and weaken U.S. energy security.

Consumer advocates and some Democrats rejected that argument, saying the industry continued to benefit from favorable tax treatment despite being among the most profitable sectors in the economy. They said the companies should contribute more at a time when households, truckers, airlines and small businesses were being squeezed by fuel costs.

The vote left Congress without a clear path forward on energy legislation, even as lawmakers from both parties acknowledged voter pressure to act. Democrats said they would continue pushing measures to curb speculation, repeal oil subsidies and invest in alternatives. Republicans said they would keep pressing for expanded drilling and production.

With gasoline prices remaining a dominant issue, both parties appeared eager to carry the fight into the campaign season. Democrats cast Republicans as allies of Big Oil, while Republicans accused Democrats of blocking access to domestic energy resources.

The result was another legislative stalemate — and no immediate relief for drivers.
